CONSCIENCE - CHAPTER OVERVIEW
- Opening quote: "Thus conscience does make cowards of us all." (William Shakespeare, Hamlet)
- We use the word conscience in everyday speech: "I've a guilty conscience", "My conscience is clear about that issue", "Have you any conscience at all?", "Is your conscience getting at you?"
- Common descriptions of conscience: a little voice inside my head guiding me; a feeling within when I am making a decision; something I feel when I do something wrong; my parents'/guardians' opinions within me; something that belongs to the past.
- The chapter covers: perspectives on conscience, the Catholic definition, moral theories, how conscience develops, an informed conscience, guilt, amorality and immorality, moral immaturity, a healthy conscience, and conflict with civil and religious authority.

PERSPECTIVES ON CONSCIENCE
- The idea of conscience is found in many peoples and races, religious or not. The Greeks, other philosophers and many modern people describe an inner law they seek to follow.
- Modern writers speak not so much of HAVING a conscience as BEING a conscience.
- Lonergan: conscience "is the means by which we achieve our fulfilment in accordance with reasonable judgement."
- Donal Harrington: conscience is our "internal moral system". Conscience is not just about deciding what to DO, but what to BE. Every decision (go to work or stay in bed, tell a lie or the truth, how to treat friends, what to do for Lent) is a decision about the kind of person we want to be.
- It may be easier to think of conscience as part of what a person is, not something a person has.
- Linda Hogan: conscience is the "personal discernment of good and evil in the context of a relationship with a loving God". It uses our thoughts, feelings, emotions and imagination to come to a decision.
- Two levels: we use conscience to judge an action ("my conscience tells me it is wrong to bully someone"); at a deeper level it is our awareness of ourselves as moral people who can be called to account by others, by ourselves and by God ("my conscience is guiding me to be a good person").

THE CATHOLIC CHURCH'S DEFINITION OF CONSCIENCE
- The Catechism of the Catholic Church (CCC 1776), quoting Gaudium et spes of Vatican II: "Deep within our conscience we discover a law which... we must obey. Its voice, ever calling us to love and to do what is good and to avoid evil, sounds in our heart at the right moment... For we have in our heart a law inscribed by God... Conscience is our most secret core and sanctuary. There we are alone with God whose voice echoes in our depths."
- So conscience is: a law deep within the person; a voice that sounds in the heart.
- What it says: it calls us to love; it encourages us to do good and avoid evil; it judges our actions.
- Where it comes from: written by God in the heart, the place where the person and God meet.
- How it is shaped: formed with reference to the supreme Good to which we are drawn - for the Catholic Christian, that is God.
- Obligation: we must follow faithfully what we know to be just and right. A human being must always obey the certain judgement of his/her conscience.

MORAL THEORIES AND CONSCIENCE
- A person's moral theory influences how they define conscience.
- Deontological model: conscience keeps before us the eternal laws of God and the human being.
- Teleological model: conscience keeps before us our ultimate end.
- Relational model: conscience keeps before us our relationships with self, neighbour and God.

DEVELOPING CONSCIENCE
- The awakening and development of conscience is gradual: it begins in childhood and continues all through life.
- Early years: behaviour is motivated by pleasure and pain, reward and punishment. No conscience at work yet ("If I cry, I'll get my way!").
- From about age six or seven: children obey laws their parents set and slowly understand the reasons and values behind them; they begin to act a certain way because it is right.
- 'Mirror conscience': picking up from parents/guardians what is right and wrong. Slowly we find our own sense of right and wrong; we may notice hypocrisy in adult behaviour; we find our own moral compass.
- Analogy: like learning to speak a language. We all have an innate ability to speak but it develops differently; accents reflect where we come from but still differ from person to person.
- We are conditioned to some extent by our community, but we also become our own people. Conscience emerges as a person grows.
- Development is influenced by the home, the community and the law, leading the person to know what brings real happiness. It is linked to the growth of the whole person: emotionally, physically and intellectually.
- Motivation moves from reward/punishment, through the need for affirmation and self-worth, toward acting simply out of personal conviction.
- In reality we act from all these motivations throughout life (selfishly for ease, to be liked, or because it is right). We are complex beings. (Kohlberg's theory of moral development is covered in chapter 11.)

AN INFORMED CONSCIENCE
- Informed conscience: a conscience we have made an effort to educate so that we learn in our hearts what is right and wrong.
- Why? Otherwise we may simply rely on our own feelings. We need to learn from wisdom outside ourselves.
- Key phrase: "We decide for ourselves, but we do not decide by ourselves."
- We can be lazy and selfish and deaden our conscience. Example: "My conscience tells me that it's fine not to sit the exams because the whole system is corrupt" - this could be a principled position or an excuse for laziness.
- A morally mature person moves away from self-interest toward decisions based on values and principles. Example: "I will follow my conscience and not take a bribe to get someone planning permission!"
- Informing conscience involves: listening to what others have learnt before us; listening to people we respect in the world around us.
- Example: deciding whether to keep a person on a life-support machine - seek medical advice, reflect on faith teaching, talk to people who have been in a similar situation, reflect on what the person would want.
- Virtue ethics: using wisdom, courage, justice and balance to make decisions (studied in chapter 11). Aristotle: a rounded moral judgement is ever the work of a virtuous person.
- 'Hearing voices': family, friends, teachers, neighbours, books, movies and music are all influences on our hearts. But in a well-formed and healthy conscience, the final say is our own.
- Irish Bishops, Conscience (1998): "Being aware of how an issue appears to my friends, how other people in my community, past and present, have understood it, helps me to make the best, most informed decision."

AN INFORMED CHRISTIAN CONSCIENCE
- A Christian conscience is informed by:
- listening to the Word of God in scripture;
- learning from taking part in the sacraments;
- listening to the teaching of the Church;
- letting God's Spirit work through prayer;
- looking at the lives of good people.
- CCC 1785: the Word of God is the light for our path; we must assimilate it in faith and prayer and put it into practice; examine our conscience before the Lord's Cross; we are assisted by the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the witness or advice of others, and the authoritative teaching of the Church.
- Informing conscience is not just getting advice on a problem; it is about being the right person. For the Christian, conscience is affected most of all by the relationship with Christ.
- Example: a Christian voting in a referendum on the proposed EU Constitution would learn about the issue but also reflect on their faith, what Christ and the Church teach, and pray.

CLEAR CONSCIENCE AND GUILT
- Conscience guides us toward the person we are meant to become.
- When our actions are true to who we are meant to be, we experience the peace and joy of a good conscience.
- When our actions work against our growth or the Law written in our hearts, we experience remorse or guilt.
- Feelings are morally neutral. It is not wrong to feel sad, angry, depressed or upset; it is our ACTIONS that carry moral value.
- Example: someone gossips unfairly about your friend; feeling angry is not wrong, but throwing a punch is.
- Guilt can be a guide that something has gone wrong; a healthy conscience keeps us on track.
- Some people carry an unhealthy burden of guilt and find it hard to let go of remorse and know forgiveness and healing.
- Christian teaching: ultimately one is judged on whether one did what one sincerely believed to be the right thing.

THE ABSENCE OF CONSCIENCE: AMORALITY
- Amorality: the absence of the moral. An amoral person has absolutely no concept of good or evil and does not see any moral element in their actions.
- Example: people involved in genocide - to try to wipe out a race, a person must deny any common humanity or right to life with dignity.
- Amoral people are guided not by right or wrong but by their own reward, safety or need for power.

IMMORALITY
- Immoral is the opposite of moral. An immoral act breaks a moral law or acts against a moral good (e.g. to kill, steal, lie about another person).
- An immoral person constantly breaks the moral law; their fundamental direction in life is against what is good.
- Difference from amoral: an immoral person DOES believe in right and wrong but consciously chooses to do wrong. Example: someone who lives a life of crime fully aware it is wrong.

MORAL IMMATURITY
- Morally immature: a person whose sense of morality/conscience is not well developed; the opposite of a conscientious person.
- Examples:
- someone who believes, because of their environment, that stealing is acceptable;
- an emotionally insecure person who follows others: "I thought that it was wrong, but everyone is doing it, so it must be okay";
- someone too busy with work to reflect on their family relationships breaking down;
- an alcoholic who refuses to admit the problem and its effect on the family.
- Usual reasons: they have not learned how to be moral in their decisions, or they have not developed an ability to reflect and work things out.
- The conscientious person is thoughtful and listens sensitively to what is happening in the world.
- What blocks this in the morally immature person is often IGNORANCE and BIAS.
- Bias example: a totally biased football supporter who blames the ref and says the others cheated; an honest observer sees the situation in a balanced way.
- Bias dulls moral judgement; seen most clearly in racism and stereotyping.
- Case study 'Cead Mile Failte!' (Kerryman, 28 August 2003): a Nigerian-born businesswoman in Tralee, foodstore owner Lara Olukunle, received a third handwritten hate letter threatening to machine gun every pregnant African woman in the town, using racist language.

A HEALTHY CONSCIENCE
- Bernard Haring: "The most precious thing on earth is a healthy, alert and faithful conscience, free for others, free for all moral values, and able to discern the scale and urgency of values."
- To have a healthy conscience we need to reflect: to make time to think things out and be present to ourselves.
- Following conscience can require honesty and courage; acting on conscience means truly taking responsibility for your actions.
- A healthy conscience hears all the voices and still keeps its freedom. Listen, then make up your own mind.
- Image of the artist: the conscientious person is like a chef, artist or composer - they learn the rules and then use their conscience in their own creative way. Conscience does not grow simply by following rules; it must be nurtured to develop the mature person.
- Mark Twain: "In a crucial moral emergency, a sound heart is a safer guide than an ill-trained conscience."
- Exercise cases: Mick steals 50 euro from his mother and feels very guilty; Fiona cons an elderly client out of 100,000 euro and doesn't care; Catherine is having an affair she knows should end; Jack is a scrupulous man ashamed of getting angry once at work; Brian discovers he is helping launder money but stays quiet though it worries him.

CONSCIENCE AND CIVIL AUTHORITY
- When deciding, we must take account of the wisdom of others and also the civil law, which exists for the common good of the whole community.
- Civil law does not cover every moral decision: in Western society there is no law against telling lies or committing adultery, yet these are immoral.
- Sometimes obeying the law would mean acting against conscience. A 'bad' law can go against conscience, e.g. oppression of a minority. Discrimination against Jews in Germany in the 1930s was state law but led to great evil.
- Serving in the army for an unjust war: when war is declared people may be conscripted. If a person believes the war is unjust, or is a total pacifist, there is a conflict between conscience and the State.
- Conscientious objector: a person who refuses, for reasons of conscience, to fight in a war. Many countries let them serve society in another role, but not all. It takes great courage; they may be seen as cowardly or unpatriotic.
- Religious freedom: the right to believe and live out one's faith. Not every country accepts it; in some places certain faiths are illegal. Conscience suggests one can and should, if at all possible, refuse to cooperate with an unjust law.
- People who risked all to follow conscience: Joan of Arc, Martin Luther King, Alexander Solzhenitsyn.
- Classic example: St Thomas More, who went to his death rather than accept King Henry VIII as head of the Church - acting out of an informed conscience against the law of the land.

CONSCIENCE AND RELIGIOUS AUTHORITY
- Magisterium: the teaching authority of the Catholic Church. It teaches Catholics in matters of faith and morals so that there is the same belief and practice throughout the Church.
- Latin for obeying is 'obedire', meaning to listen. The great command begins "Hear O Israel". To obey God is not blind obedience but listening to one who loves us; Catholics do this together as a church.
- Alongside this there is respect for the person's conscience. People sharing the same faith will have different opinions. A person's conscience comes first, but it must be as fully informed as possible.
- This balance can cause difficulty: religious authorities teach the primacy of conscience while also teaching truths of faith and morals. Who finally decides God's will for a believer - the Magisterium or the individual's conscience? There have been different emphases through history.
- John Henry Cardinal Newman: "I shall drink - to the Pope, if you please - still to Conscience first, and to the Pope afterwards."
- This is NOT the same as doing your own thing. An informed conscience listens closely to tradition, the Holy Spirit, the wisdom of church teaching through the ages and the Church's current position.
- If disagreement remains: "A conscience can go astray through ignorance without thereby losing its dignity." (Gaudium et spes, The Church in the Modern World, 16)
- Sullivan, Magisterium: the sincere Catholic who genuinely tries to listen to Church teaching but still disagrees has done all they can to assent and should not be condemned for lacking obedience.
- Linda Hogan: the Church must live with the contradictions that flow from its teaching on conscience. Some emphasise obedience, others freedom; both are involved. Disagreement and diversity will always be part of the Church's moral life.

DIFFERENT LEVELS OF TEACHING
- The Irish Bishops' Conference document on the economy, Work is the Key / Prosperity with a Purpose, does not teach with complete authority - people will have different views on job creation.
- When the Pope teaches in Evangelium vitae that direct and voluntary killing is always gravely immoral, it is with greater authority.
- Bishops sometimes advise how Christians ought to vote but always add that Christians must follow their informed conscience.
- Abortion referendum, March 2002: the Catholic Church taught the best result would be a Yes vote, which would reverse the X case (which at the time allowed abortion in the case of a suicidal mother). Document: 'An Opportunity not to be Lost', Episcopal Conference, March 2002.
- Many Catholics did not accept this and campaigned for a No vote, judging a Yes vote would eventually allow abortion in certain cases. Other Catholics voted No so abortion would be allowed in certain cases. Each group claimed to be faithful to the Church while exercising freedom of conscience.

SUMMARY
- Conscience is a voice deep within a person calling them to do good and avoid evil. It is about being as much as doing.
- Conscience develops as people grow.
- An informed conscience listens and reflects on the wisdom of the community.
- Christian conscience is formed by the Word of God and the living tradition of the Christian community.
- Amorality is the absence of a sense of good and evil.
- Moral immaturity stems from a lack of development of conscience.
- Following one's conscience can bring conflict with civil and religious authority.

KEY TERMS
- Conscience: the law and voice deep within a person calling them to love, do good and avoid evil, and judging their actions.
- Informed conscience: a conscience educated by listening to wisdom outside oneself before deciding.
- Amorality: the absence of any sense of good and evil.
- Immoral act: an act that breaks a moral law or goes against a moral good.
- Morally immature: having a poorly developed conscience, often due to ignorance and bias.
- Conscientious objector: someone who refuses, for reasons of conscience, to fight in a war.
- Magisterium: the teaching authority of the Catholic Church in faith and morals.
- Mirror conscience: an early conscience that copies parents'/guardians' sense of right and wrong.

rows.prompt: Explain what Donal Harrington means when he says conscience is about 'what to be', not just 'what to do'.
rows.model_answer: Every decision we make, like telling the truth or how we treat friends, shapes the kind of person we are becoming. So conscience is not only judging single actions; it is our awareness of ourselves as moral people. It is part of who we are, not just something we have.

rows.prompt: According to the Catholic Church, what does the voice of conscience tell us? Name three things.
rows.model_answer: It calls us to love. It encourages us to do good and avoid evil. It judges our actions. It is a law written by God in the heart, where the person and God meet.

rows.prompt: Outline the stages in the development of conscience.
rows.model_answer: In early childhood behaviour is driven by pleasure and pain, reward and punishment. From about six or seven children obey their parents' rules and begin to understand why, starting with a 'mirror conscience'. Motivation then moves through the need for affirmation and self-worth toward acting out of personal conviction.

rows.prompt: What does 'an informed conscience' mean? Give an example.
rows.model_answer: An informed conscience is one we have educated by listening to the wisdom of others before deciding: we decide for ourselves, but not by ourselves. For example, a family deciding about a life-support machine would ask medical experts, reflect on their faith, talk to people in a similar situation and think about what the person would want.

rows.prompt: Name three ways a Christian informs their conscience.
rows.model_answer: By listening to the Word of God in scripture, by taking part in the sacraments, and by listening to the teaching of the Church. They also let God's Spirit work through prayer and look at the lives of good people. Above all, conscience is shaped by their relationship with Christ.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between an amoral person and an immoral person.
rows.model_answer: An amoral person has no concept of good or evil and sees no moral element in their actions, like those involved in genocide. An immoral person believes in right and wrong but consciously chooses to do wrong, like someone who lives a life of crime fully aware it is wrong.

rows.prompt: Describe a morally immature person and give one example.
rows.model_answer: A morally immature person has a conscience that is not well developed, often because of ignorance and bias or because they have never learned to reflect. For example, an insecure person who thinks 'everyone is doing it, so it must be okay', or an alcoholic who refuses to admit their problem.

rows.prompt: What did Cardinal Newman mean by drinking a toast 'to Conscience first, and to the Pope afterwards'?
rows.model_answer: Newman meant that a person's informed conscience comes first, even before Church authority. This does not mean doing your own thing; an informed conscience listens closely to Church teaching and tradition. But the final judgement belongs to the person's conscience.

rows.prompt: 'We decide for ourselves, but we do not decide by ourselves.' Discuss this statement with reference to the formation of an informed Christian conscience. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: An informed conscience is one that a person has made an effort to educate so they learn in their heart what is right and wrong. If we do not inform our conscience we may simply rely on our feelings, or deaden it out of laziness or self-interest. We decide for ourselves because, in a healthy conscience, the final say is our own; but we do not decide by ourselves because we listen to what others have learnt before us and to people we respect. The Irish Bishops (1998) say knowing how an issue appears to friends and to the community past and present helps us make the best decision. Virtue ethics adds that we use wisdom, courage, justice and balance. A Christian conscience is also informed by listening to the Word of God in scripture, taking part in the sacraments, listening to Church teaching, praying, and looking at the lives of good people. CCC 1785 says the Word of God is 'the light for our path' and we are guided by the gifts of the Holy Spirit and the teaching of the Church. Most of all, a Christian conscience is shaped by a relationship with Christ, because it is about being the right person, not just getting the right information. For example, a Christian voting on the EU Constitution would study the issue, reflect on Christ's and the Church's teaching, and pray.

rows.prompt: Describe how conscience develops from childhood to adulthood. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: The development of conscience is gradual, beginning in childhood and continuing through life. In the early years a child is motivated by pleasure and pain, reward and punishment; there is no conscience at work ('If I cry, I'll get my way!'). From about six or seven, children obey the rules their parents set and slowly begin to understand the values behind them, so they start to act because it is right. At first this is a 'mirror conscience': picking up right and wrong from parents or guardians. Slowly a young person finds their own sense of right and wrong; they may notice hypocrisy in adults and begin to find their own moral compass. This is like learning a language: everyone can speak, but accents differ. We are shaped by our community but become our own people. Development is influenced by home, community and law, and is linked to growth of the whole person: emotionally, physically and intellectually. Motivation moves from reward and punishment, through the need for affirmation and self-worth, toward acting out of personal conviction. In reality we act from all these motives throughout life, because we are complex beings. A mature conscience must be nurtured, not simply follow rules, like an artist who learns the rules and then uses them creatively.

rows.prompt: Explain, using examples, how following one's conscience can bring a person into conflict with civil authority. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Civil law exists for the common good and must be taken into account when making moral decisions. But it does not cover every moral matter: there is no Western law against lying or adultery, though they are immoral. Sometimes obeying the law would mean acting against conscience, because a 'bad' law may oppress a minority. In Germany in the 1930s discrimination against Jews was state law but led to great evil. A second example is conscription in time of war. If a person believes a war is unjust, or is a total pacifist, they face a conflict between conscience and the State. Some countries allow a conscientious objector to serve society in another way, but not all, and such a person may be seen as cowardly or unpatriotic, so it takes great courage. A third example is religious freedom, the right to believe and live out one's faith. Some countries make certain faiths illegal; conscience suggests one should, if at all possible, refuse to cooperate with an unjust law. History gives examples of people who risked everything for conscience: Joan of Arc, Martin Luther King and Alexander Solzhenitsyn. The classic example is St Thomas More, who went to his death rather than accept King Henry VIII as head of the Church, acting from an informed conscience against the law of the land.

Obeying comes from 'obedire', to listen, so obedience is not blind but listening to one who loves us. Alongside this the Church respects conscience: a person's conscience comes first, but it must be fully informed. Newman toasted 'Conscience first, and the Pope afterwards'. This is not doing your own thing. If a sincere Catholic still disagrees, Gaudium et spes 16 says conscience 'can go astray through ignorance without thereby losing its dignity'.
